templates.name: Present or describe to an already familiar audience
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Specify or identify a single fact

items.subtype: Explain why (cause over a chain of bullets)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tiger beetles are predatory insects that chase small arthropods over open, sandy landscapes.
• During a chase, a tiger beetle repeatedly stops for a fraction of a second before accelerating again.
• At top speed, the beetle’s eyes cannot take in sufficient light to form a recognizable image.
• During each momentary stop, its vision recovers, allowing it to locate the prey again.
• While sprinting, tiger beetles hold their antennae stiffly out in front to detect obstacles by touch.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why tiger beetles stop repeatedly while chasing prey. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Tiger beetles stop repeatedly during a chase because their stiffly held antennae cannot detect obstacles at top speed, forcing them to feel their way forward.
Holding their antennae stiffly out in front, tiger beetles detect obstacles by touch as they sprint after small arthropods over open landscapes.
Because a tiger beetle at top speed cannot see its prey clearly, it stops briefly during a chase to let its vision recover and locate the prey again.
At top speed, a tiger beetle’s eyes cannot take in sufficient light to form a recognizable image of anything in front of it.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain why the beetles keep stopping. The notes link two facts: at top speed the beetle’s eyes cannot form a sharp image, and during each brief stop its vision recovers so it can relocate the prey. Choice C joins them into a cause and its effect.

A.why_wrong: The notes say the antennae detect obstacles while the beetle is sprinting; they do not say the antennae fail at top speed or that the beetle stops because of them.

B.why_wrong: It describes how the beetles use their antennae while running, but it says nothing about why they stop during a pursuit.

D.why_wrong: It gives the problem with the beetle’s vision but never connects it to the stops, so it does not explain why the beetles stop repeatedly.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (insect vision and pursuit). Real phenomenon known without a search (tiger beetles outrun their own vision and pause to relocate prey; antennae held forward to sense obstacles); attributed to no named researcher (WAVE.md, no fact-checking for this skill). Band 6 by plan: one goal-shaped FALSE, one OG, one PART that gives the cause without the link.

band7.why: EXPL with one goal-shaped FALSE (wrong cause), one OG, one PART; key paraphrases the vision bullets; a solid band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Present the findings (two findings, strike type mapped to prey)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ogre-faced spiders are nocturnal predators that snare prey with a small silk net stretched between their front legs.
• Two of their eight eyes are enormous and extraordinarily sensitive to dim light.
• The spiders capture walking insects with forward strikes and flying insects with backward strikes.
• In one study, biologists covered the two large eyes with dental silicone and compared the spiders’ hunting performance with that of uncovered individuals.
• Spiders with covered eyes made far fewer successful forward strikes than uncovered spiders did, but their backward strikes succeeded about as often.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The biologists found that covering the spiders’ eyes sharply reduced how often they caught flying insects but had little effect on how often they caught walking ones.
Covering the spiders’ eyes sharply reduced how often they caught walking insects but had little effect on how often they caught flying ones, the biologists found.
Biologists compared the hunting performance of ogre-faced spiders whose large eyes they had covered with dental silicone with that of uncovered spiders.
The biologists found that spiders with covered eyes caught both walking and flying insects less often than uncovered spiders did.
items.explanation: The notes give the findings in terms of strikes: covered spiders made far fewer successful forward strikes, but their backward strikes succeeded about as often. Forward strikes catch walking insects and backward strikes catch flying ones, so covering the eyes hurt the capture of walking insects and barely affected the capture of flying insects. Choice B presents both findings and attaches each to the right kind of prey.

A.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: findings reversed, strike type mapped to the wrong prey)
A.why_wrong: Forward strikes, the ones that suffered, are used on walking insects; backward strikes, used on flying insects, succeeded about as often as before. The effects are attached to the wrong prey.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the biologists ran the study, not what they found.

D.why_wrong: Only the forward strikes, used on walking insects, became less successful; backward strikes, used on flying insects, succeeded about as often as in uncovered spiders.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (sensory ecology). Real, identifiable research setting (net-casting ogre-faced spiders, forward strikes at walking prey and backward strikes at flying prey, the two large eyes covered with dental silicone); the team is unnamed and the findings are stated qualitatively, consistent with the pattern the real study is known for, with no invented figures; the forward and backward strike mapping is general natural history, not verified by search (search budget exhausted during review, 2026-10-20). Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped (mapping reversed), D FALSE goal-shaped (drop extended to flying prey), C true but off-goal. Goal-only solve (notes hidden): A, B and D all present findings.
band7_moves: present-the-findings goal over two findings that point opposite ways (vision matters for walking prey, not for flying prey)
findings stated as strike types; the key restates them as prey types, so the student must map forward strike to walking prey and backward strike to flying prey
two goal-shaped FALSE options that present both findings: one reverses the mapping, one extends the drop to both prey

fixes: replaced the invented percentages (80%, 40%) with qualitative findings, since the study is real and identifiable
added a strike-type bullet and restated the findings as forward and backward strikes so the key maps strikes to prey
rewrote options A and D as goal-shaped FALSE options without numbers and matched C to the new wording; updated explanation, distractors, subtype, band7_moves, notes, word_count (106 words)

band7.why: Present-the-findings over two findings that point opposite ways; key derived by mapping strike type to prey; two goal-shaped FALSE options (reversed mapping, overextension) and one OG; goal-only solve leaves A, B and D.

items.subtype: Historical overview of an event
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Golden Stool, sacred symbol of the Asante people of present-day Ghana, is traditionally never sat upon.
• In 1900, Britain’s colonial governor demanded that the Asante surrender the stool.
• Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, then organized an armed resistance known as the War of the Golden Stool.
• Her forces besieged the British fort at Kumasi for months before colonial reinforcements suppressed the uprising.
• Britain exiled Yaa Asantewaa and annexed the Asante kingdom in 1902, but the carefully concealed stool was never surrendered.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the War of the Golden Stool. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: During the War of the Golden Stool, forces led by Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, besieged the British fort at Kumasi for months.
After the Asante surrendered their sacred Golden Stool to Britain’s governor in 1900, Yaa Asantewaa led a rebellion that ended with Britain annexing the Asante kingdom in 1902.
The Golden Stool, which is traditionally never sat upon, is the sacred symbol of the Asante people of present-day Ghana.
Sparked by Britain’s 1900 demand for the Golden Stool, Yaa Asantewaa’s rebellion was eventually suppressed, yet the sacred stool itself was never surrendered.
items.explanation: An overview of the war has to cover how it began, how it ended and what became of the stool at its center. Choice D gives the British demand that started it, its suppression, and the fact that the Asante never gave up the stool, all of which the notes support.

A.why_wrong: It describes only the siege of Kumasi; it leaves out what started the war and how it ended, so it is not an overview.

B.why_wrong: The notes say the governor demanded the stool and that it was never surrendered; the rebellion followed the demand, not a surrender.

C.why_wrong: It explains what the Golden Stool is, but it says nothing about the war itself.

items.notes: Subject: history (Asante resistance to British rule, 1900). Facts are general history known without a search (the governor’s 1900 demand for the stool, Yaa Asantewaa’s rising and the siege of the Kumasi fort, her exile, annexation in 1902, the stool hidden and never handed over). Band 6 by plan: PART, one goal-shaped FALSE, OG.

band7.why: OVERVIEW with PART, one goal-shaped FALSE (stool surrendered) and OG; key spans cause, outcome and the stool across three bullets; band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Present findings to an audience familiar with a method
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Radiocarbon dating estimates the age of organic material by measuring how much carbon-14 it retains.
• In 1913, archaeologists excavating an ancient cemetery at Tarkhan, Egypt, recovered a bundle of linen.
• Conservators later discovered that it contained a pleated garment, now known as the Tarkhan Dress.
• In 2016, researchers reported that radiocarbon analysis dated the linen to between 3482 and 3102 BCE.
• That result makes the Tarkhan Dress the oldest known woven garment in the world.
items.stem: The student wants to present the 2016 findings to an audience already familiar with radiocarbon dating. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Researchers reported in 2016 that radiocarbon analysis dated the Tarkhan Dress’s linen to between 3482 and 3102 BCE, making it the world’s oldest known woven garment.
Radiocarbon dating, which estimates the age of organic material from the carbon-14 it retains, showed in 2016 that the Tarkhan Dress was made between 3482 and 3102 BCE.
The Tarkhan Dress, a pleated linen garment, was recovered from an ancient Egyptian cemetery in 1913 and only later recognized by conservators.
In 2016, researchers used radiocarbon analysis to estimate the age of the linen from which the Tarkhan Dress was made.
items.explanation: An audience familiar with radiocarbon dating needs only the result: the dress’s linen dates to between 3482 and 3102 BCE, which makes it the oldest known woven garment. Choice A gives that result without explaining the method.

B.why_wrong: It defines radiocarbon dating, which this audience already understands, and it leaves out what makes the date significant.

C.why_wrong: It tells how and when the dress was found, not what the 2016 analysis showed.

D.why_wrong: It says that researchers dated the linen but not what date they found or what the date means.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (oldest woven garment). Real object and result known without a search (excavated by Petrie’s team at Tarkhan in 1913, recognized as a dress by conservators decades later, radiocarbon date reported in 2016); no researcher named. Band 6 by plan: AUD, OG, PART, as in 3.7.

band7.why: AUD_FAM has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; AUD, OG, PART as in 39ccb463; a fair band 6.

items.subtype: Explanation and example
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sortition is the selection of people for public decision-making by random lottery rather than by election.
• Advocates argue that randomly selected bodies can represent a population more accurately than legislatures.
• In 2004, British Columbia, Canada, gathered 160 residents chosen by lottery into a Citizens’ Assembly.
• Members spent nearly a year studying electoral systems before recommending a new one for the province.
• A 2005 referendum on the recommendation fell just short of the required 60% approval.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of sortition. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In 2004, British Columbia formed a Citizens’ Assembly whose members studied electoral systems for nearly a year before recommending a new one.
Sortition, in which voters decide a question directly instead of electing representatives, was used in British Columbia’s 2005 referendum on a new electoral system.
Sortition, the use of a random lottery rather than an election to select decision-makers, was used in 2004 when British Columbia chose 160 residents to form a Citizens’ Assembly.
Advocates of sortition, which selects people for public decision-making by lottery, argue that such bodies represent a population better than legislatures do.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: say what sortition is and give an instance of it. Choice C defines sortition as choosing decision-makers by lottery instead of election and names British Columbia’s 2004 Citizens’ Assembly, whose 160 members were chosen that way.

A.why_wrong: It describes the Citizens’ Assembly but never explains sortition or says the members were chosen by lottery.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: wrong definition and wrong example)
B.why_wrong: Sortition is selection by lottery, not voters deciding a question directly; the referendum was a vote, not an example of sortition.

D.why_wrong: It explains sortition and what its advocates claim, but it gives no example.

items.notes: Subject: social science (democratic institutions). Real case known without a search (British Columbia’s 2004 Citizens’ Assembly on Electoral Reform, 160 members drawn by lot, 2005 referendum near 58% against a 60% threshold). Plan cell asked for band 7, but EXAMPLE has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md), so written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md: two PART options, one goal-shaped FALSE.

band7.why: EXAMPLE has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; PART, goal-shaped FALSE, PART as in ec03f090; a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Difference on a named attribute
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Nearly all glass is made primarily of silica, the main component of sand.
• Soda-lime glass, used for windows and bottles, accounts for most of the glass manufactured worldwide.
• It expands considerably when heated, so a sudden temperature change can crack it.
• Borosilicate glass contains boron oxide, which reduces how much the glass expands when heated.
• It can therefore withstand sudden temperature changes and is used for laboratory beakers.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between how the two kinds of glass respond to sudden temperature changes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both soda-lime glass and borosilicate glass are made primarily of silica, the main component of sand.
Borosilicate glass contains boron oxide, a substance that reduces how much the glass expands when it is heated.
Soda-lime glass, which accounts for most of the glass manufactured worldwide, is used for windows and bottles, whereas borosilicate glass is used for laboratory beakers.
Unlike soda-lime glass, which a sudden temperature change can crack, borosilicate glass can withstand such changes.
items.explanation: The goal names one attribute: how each glass responds to a sudden change in temperature. Choice D contrasts the two on exactly that point: soda-lime glass can crack, while borosilicate glass withstands the change.

A.recipe: REL (a similarity offered for a difference)
A.why_wrong: It states what the two kinds of glass have in common rather than how they differ.

B.recipe: PART (one kind of glass, and its cause rather than its response)
B.why_wrong: It describes only borosilicate glass and never compares it with soda-lime glass.

C.why_wrong: It contrasts how the two kinds of glass are used, not how they respond to sudden temperature changes.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (materials). General chemistry known without a search (soda-lime is the common glass; boron oxide lowers thermal expansion, so borosilicate resists thermal shock). Distractors: REL (both), PART, REL on the wrong dimension (uses).

items.subtype: Contrast two artists on one attribute
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bharti Kher and Subodh Gupta are contemporary artists based in New Delhi, India.
• Both incorporate everyday objects associated with Indian domestic life into their sculptures.
• Kher frequently covers her sculptures’ surfaces with bindis, decorative dots traditionally worn on the forehead.
• Gupta assembles many of his sculptures from stainless steel pots, pans, and tiffin boxes.
• His Very Hungry God (2006) is an enormous human skull constructed from steel kitchen utensils.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast the materials Kher and Gupta use in their sculptures. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Kher covers her sculptures with bindis, whereas Gupta builds many of his from stainless steel pots, pans, and tiffin boxes.
Both Kher and Gupta incorporate everyday objects associated with Indian domestic life into their sculptures.
Although both artists are based in New Delhi, Kher and Gupta use very different materials in their sculptures.
Gupta’s Very Hungry God (2006) is an enormous human skull constructed from stainless steel kitchen utensils.
items.explanation: To contrast the artists’ materials, the sentence must name the material each one uses. Choice A does: Kher covers her sculptures with bindis, while Gupta builds his from steel kitchenware.

B.recipe: REL (a similarity offered for a contrast)
B.why_wrong: It states what the two artists have in common, not how their materials differ.

C.recipe: VAGUE (says the materials differ without naming them)
C.why_wrong: It asserts that the artists use different materials but never says what those materials are.

D.why_wrong: It describes one of Gupta’s works and says nothing about Kher’s materials.

items.notes: Subject: arts (contemporary Indian sculpture). Real artists and well-known facts, no search needed (Kher’s bindi works; Gupta’s steel utensil sculptures, Very Hungry God 2006; both based in New Delhi). Distractors: REL, VAGUE, PART.

items.subtype: Describe an invention to an audience unfamiliar with the inventor
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Granville T. Woods (1856–1910) was an African American inventor and electrical engineer.
• He received more than fifty patents, many of them for electrical equipment used by railways.
• In 1887, Woods patented the induction telegraph.
• This system allowed messages to be transmitted between moving trains and nearby railway stations.
• It reduced the risk of collisions by alerting train crews to hazards ahead.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the induction telegraph to an audience unfamiliar with Granville T. Woods. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Woods’s induction telegraph, patented in 1887, allowed messages to be transmitted between moving trains and nearby railway stations.
Patented in 1887 by African American inventor Granville T. Woods, the induction telegraph allowed messages to pass between moving trains and railway stations.
African American inventor and electrical engineer Granville T. Woods, who lived from 1856 to 1910, received more than fifty patents, many of them for railway equipment.
The system that Woods patented in 1887 reduced the risk of collisions by alerting train crews to hazards ahead.
items.explanation: For readers who do not know Woods, the sentence has to say who he was and also describe his invention. Choice B identifies Woods as an African American inventor and explains what the induction telegraph did.

A.why_wrong: It describes the telegraph but refers to “Woods” without saying who he was, which this audience would need.

C.recipe: OG (introduces the inventor, not the invention)
C.why_wrong: It identifies Woods but never mentions or describes the induction telegraph.

D.why_wrong: It refers to Woods without saying who he was, and it never names the induction telegraph, so this audience learns neither who Woods was nor which invention is meant.

items.notes: Subject: history (inventors). Real person and well-known facts, no search needed (Woods, 1856 to 1910; more than fifty patents; induction telegraph patented 1887 for communication with moving trains). Distractors: AUD, OG, AUD.

fixes: corrected D's why_wrong: D does describe the system's effect but never introduces Woods or names the telegraph

items.subtype: Describe a work to an audience unfamiliar with the artist
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lee Bul is a South Korean artist whose sculptures and performances often challenge conventional ideals of beauty.
• Her installation Majestic Splendor was exhibited in 1997 at New York City’s Museum of Modern Art.
• It consisted of raw fish decorated with sequins and beads and sealed inside transparent plastic bags.
• As the fish decomposed, the odor became so strong that the museum removed the installation.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Majestic Splendor to an audience unfamiliar with Lee Bul. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Majestic Splendor consisted of raw fish that had been decorated with sequins and beads and then sealed inside transparent plastic bags.
Lee Bul is a South Korean artist whose sculptures and performances often challenge conventional ideals of beauty.
As Lee’s sequined fish decomposed, the odor became so strong that the Museum of Modern Art removed them in 1997.
Majestic Splendor, a 1997 installation by South Korean artist Lee Bul, consisted of raw fish decorated with sequins and beads and sealed in plastic bags.
items.explanation: Readers unfamiliar with Lee Bul need to be told who she is as well as what the work was. Choice D identifies her as a South Korean artist and describes Majestic Splendor: raw fish decorated with sequins and beads, sealed in plastic bags.

A.why_wrong: It describes the installation but never says who made it, so the audience learns nothing about the artist.

B.recipe: OG (introduces the artist, not the work)
B.why_wrong: It identifies Lee Bul but does not mention or describe Majestic Splendor.

C.why_wrong: It uses Lee’s name without introducing her and does not name the work or fully describe it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (installation art). Real artist and well-known episode, no search needed (Majestic Splendor, sequined fish in bags, removed from MoMA in 1997 because of the smell). Distractors: AUD, OG, AUD.

items.subtype: Emphasize the scale of a collection
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Federal Writers’ Project was a New Deal program that employed writers during the Great Depression.
• From 1936 to 1938, its interviewers recorded the life stories of formerly enslaved people.
• Altogether, they collected more than 2,300 first-person accounts in seventeen states.
• The accounts are now preserved at the Library of Congress.
• Historians caution that some interviewers altered speakers’ words or asked leading questions.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how extensive the project’s collection of life stories is. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Federal Writers’ Project, a New Deal program, employed writers during the Great Depression.
Historians caution that some interviewers for the Federal Writers’ Project altered speakers’ words or asked leading questions.
Between 1936 and 1938 alone, Federal Writers’ Project interviewers collected more than 2,300 first-person accounts from formerly enslaved people in seventeen states.
The life stories that Federal Writers’ Project interviewers recorded between 1936 and 1938 are now preserved in the collections of the Library of Congress.
items.explanation: To show how extensive the collection is, the sentence needs its size and reach. Choice C gives both: more than 2,300 accounts, gathered in seventeen states in about three years.

A.why_wrong: It describes the Federal Writers’ Project in general and says nothing about the size of the collection.

B.why_wrong: It points out a problem with some interviews rather than emphasizing how many there are.

D.why_wrong: It says when the stories were recorded and where they are kept, not how many were collected or where they came from.

items.notes: Subject: history (New Deal oral history). Real project and well-known figures, no search needed (1936 to 1938, more than 2,300 accounts, seventeen states, Library of Congress). Distractors all OG, as in most EMPH items.

items.subtype: Emphasize the uniqueness of an accomplishment
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cherokee writer John Rollin Ridge (1827–1867) moved to California in 1850.
• He worked as a journalist and in 1857 became the first editor of the Sacramento Bee newspaper.
• In 1854, he published The Life and Adventures of Joaquín Murieta.
• The novel follows a fictionalized version of a Mexican miner who turns to banditry after suffering injustice.
• It is widely considered the first novel published by a Native American writer.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the uniqueness of Ridge’s 1854 novel. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Ridge’s 1854 novel, The Life and Adventures of Joaquín Murieta, is widely considered the first novel published by a Native American writer.
Cherokee writer John Rollin Ridge became the first editor of the Sacramento Bee newspaper in 1857, three years after publishing a novel.
The Life and Adventures of Joaquín Murieta follows a fictionalized version of a Mexican miner who turns to banditry after suffering injustice.
Four years after moving to California, Cherokee writer John Rollin Ridge published The Life and Adventures of Joaquín Murieta.
items.explanation: What makes the novel unique, according to the notes, is that it is widely considered the first novel published by a Native American writer. Choice A states this.

B.why_wrong: It emphasizes a first in Ridge’s journalism career, not anything unique about his novel.

C.why_wrong: It describes what the novel is about, not what makes it unique.

D.why_wrong: It places the novel in Ridge’s life but gives nothing that sets it apart from other novels.

items.notes: Subject: literature (early Native American fiction). Real author and well-known facts, no search needed (Cherokee writer, moved to California 1850, Joaquín Murieta 1854, first editor of the Sacramento Bee 1857). Trap: B carries the word “first” for a different accomplishment, as 2.14 D carries “Before moving to Harlem.”

items.subtype: Explain how (mechanism)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bidriware is a metal handicraft that originated in the city of Bidar, India, in the 1300s.
• Artisans cast objects such as vases and boxes from an alloy of zinc and copper.
• They engrave designs into the surface and inlay the grooves with silver.
• Finally, they rub each object with a paste containing soil from Bidar’s ancient fort.
• The paste turns the alloy a deep black but leaves the silver untouched.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how bidriware artisans make the silver designs stand out. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Bidriware, a metal handicraft that originated in the city of Bidar, India, in the 1300s, is cast into vases, boxes, and other objects from an alloy of zinc and copper.
Artisans make the silver designs on bidriware stand out with a soil paste that blackens the surrounding alloy but leaves the silver untouched.
To decorate bidriware, artisans engrave designs into the metal surface and then inlay the grooves with silver.
As a final step, bidriware artisans rub each object with a paste that contains soil from Bidar’s ancient fort.
items.explanation: The silver stands out because of a contrast the artisans create at the end: the soil paste turns the zinc and copper alloy deep black but does not change the silver. Choice B explains this.

A.why_wrong: It tells where bidriware comes from and what it is made of, not how the silver designs are made to stand out.

C.recipe: PART (how the designs are made, not how they stand out)
C.why_wrong: It explains how the silver gets into the surface but not what makes it contrast with the metal around it.

D.why_wrong: It mentions the soil paste but not what the paste does to the alloy and the silver, so it does not explain why the designs stand out.

items.notes: Subject: arts and crafts (Deccan metalwork). Real craft, facts known without a search (zinc and copper alloy, silver inlay, blackening paste made with soil from Bidar fort). Distractors: OG, PART, PART.

items.subtype: Explain why (cause)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In Earth’s atmosphere, air molecules scatter blue sunlight in every direction, making the daytime sky appear blue.
• Mars has a far thinner atmosphere that holds large quantities of fine dust.
• This dust gives the Martian daytime sky a pale, butterscotch color.
• Martian dust particles, however, scatter blue light mostly forward, close to the direction in which it is traveling.
• As a result, observers on Mars looking toward the setting Sun see a bluish glow around it.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why sunsets on Mars appear blue. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Although Mars has a far thinner atmosphere than Earth does, that atmosphere holds large quantities of fine dust, which gives the daytime sky a pale, butterscotch color.
On Earth, air molecules scatter blue sunlight in every direction, making the daytime sky appear blue.
Martian dust particles scatter blue light mostly forward, close to the direction in which it is traveling.
Because Martian dust scatters blue light mostly forward, an observer on Mars looking toward the setting Sun sees a bluish glow around it.
items.explanation: A blue sunset on Mars is explained by how its dust scatters light: blue light is sent mostly forward, so someone looking toward the setting Sun sees blue around it. Choice D links that cause to the effect.

A.why_wrong: It describes the Martian atmosphere and the color of the daytime sky, not the blue color near the setting Sun.

B.why_wrong: It explains why Earth’s daytime sky is blue, not why sunsets on Mars appear blue.

C.why_wrong: It states how Martian dust scatters blue light but never connects that to what an observer sees at sunset.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (planetary atmospheres). Real phenomenon known without a search (fine Martian dust scatters blue light forward, so sunsets look blue; photographed by NASA rovers). Distractors: two OG (true neighboring facts, as in 2.31) and one PART that gives the cause without the sunset.

items.subtype: Similarity between two practices
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In Norway, a dugnad is a session of unpaid communal work, such as neighbors cleaning shared courtyards each spring.
• Norwegian sports clubs and schools also organize dugnads to raise money.
• In Indonesia, gotong royong refers to unpaid communal work, such as villagers helping to build a neighbor’s house.
• Gotong royong is especially common in rural villages.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between dugnad and gotong royong. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both Norway’s dugnad and Indonesia’s gotong royong involve unpaid communal work, from cleaning shared courtyards to building a neighbor’s house.
In Norway, neighbors performing a dugnad might clean shared courtyards, whereas in Indonesia, villagers practicing gotong royong might build a neighbor’s house.
Norwegian sports clubs and schools organize dugnads, sessions of unpaid communal work, to raise money.
Gotong royong, a form of unpaid communal work in Indonesia, is especially common in rural villages.
items.explanation: Both practices are described as unpaid communal work. Choice A names both and states that shared trait, with an example of each.

B.recipe: REL (a difference offered for a similarity)
B.why_wrong: It contrasts the tasks done in each country instead of stating what the two practices share.

C.why_wrong: It describes one use of dugnad and does not mention gotong royong.

D.why_wrong: It describes gotong royong alone and does not compare it with dugnad.

items.notes: Subject: social science (community institutions). Real practices known without a search (dugnad as volunteer work days, including fundraising for clubs and schools; gotong royong as mutual help in Indonesian villages). Distractors: REL, PART, PART.

items.subtype: Relative degree with a derived comparison
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1976, the Helios 2 probe, a joint project of West Germany and the United States, reached about 250,000 kilometers per hour.
• For more than four decades, no spacecraft traveled faster.
• NASA launched the Parker Solar Probe in 2018 to study the Sun’s outer atmosphere.
• As it repeatedly swung close to the Sun, the probe accelerated.
• In 2021, it reached roughly 586,000 kilometers per hour.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how fast the Parker Solar Probe traveled relative to Helios 2. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Helios 2 reached about 250,000 kilometers per hour in 1976, and the Parker Solar Probe reached roughly 586,000 kilometers per hour in 2021.
Helios 2, which reached about 250,000 kilometers per hour in 1976, traveled more than twice as fast as the Parker Solar Probe.
In 2021, the Parker Solar Probe traveled more than twice as fast as Helios 2, the spacecraft that had held the speed record since 1976.
NASA launched the Parker Solar Probe in 2018 to study the outer atmosphere of the Sun.
items.explanation: The goal asks for Parker’s speed relative to Helios 2’s. The notes give about 250,000 and roughly 586,000 kilometers per hour, so Parker traveled more than twice as fast. Choice C states that comparison.

A.why_wrong: It gives both speeds side by side but never states how they compare.

B.why_wrong: Helios 2’s top speed was lower than the Parker Solar Probe’s, not higher.

D.why_wrong: It says why the probe was launched, not how fast it traveled.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (space exploration). Real missions and figures known without a search (Helios 2 record of about 250,000 km/h in 1976, beaten by Parker in 2018; about 586,000 km/h in 2021). Key derives “more than twice as fast” from the two numbers.

items.subtype: Provide an example (classification derived from the notes)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Epiphytes are plants that grow on other plants for support but take no nutrients from them.
• Spanish moss, despite its name, is not a moss but a flowering plant related to pineapples.
• It hangs in long gray strands from live oaks and cypress trees in the southeastern United States.
• It absorbs the moisture and nutrients it needs from rain and air rather than from those trees.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an example of an epiphyte. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Rather than taking nutrients from the plants that support them, epiphytes absorb what they need from other sources.
One example of an epiphyte is Spanish moss, a flowering plant that hangs in long gray strands from live oaks and cypress trees.
Many epiphytes grow on trees, which provide them with support but not with nutrients.
One example of an epiphyte is the live oak, a tree from which Spanish moss hangs in long gray strands.
items.explanation: An epiphyte grows on another plant for support but takes no nutrients from it. Spanish moss hangs from trees and draws its moisture and nutrients from rain and air, so it fits the definition. Choice B offers it as the example.

A.why_wrong: It explains how epiphytes get nutrients but names no particular epiphyte.

C.why_wrong: It says where many epiphytes grow but does not give an example of one.

D.recipe: FALSE (the host offered as the example)
D.why_wrong: The live oak is the tree Spanish moss grows on; nothing in the notes says the live oak is an epiphyte.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany). Real plant and well-known facts, no search needed (Tillandsia usneoides is a bromeliad, an epiphyte on live oaks and bald cypress, not a parasite). Key needs one step: the notes never call Spanish moss an epiphyte, as 2.42 never calls pineapple a source of “vitamin C” directly.

items.subtype: Present the aim and methodology
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Breadfruit, a starchy tree fruit, is grown widely in Jamaica, which imports nearly all of its wheat.
• Food scientists in Jamaica wanted to know whether breadfruit flour could replace part of the wheat flour in bread.
• They baked loaves in which 0, 10, 20, or 30 percent of the wheat flour was replaced with breadfruit flour.
• Fifty volunteers then rated each loaf’s flavor and texture.
• Loaves containing up to 20 percent breadfruit flour received ratings similar to those of all-wheat loaves.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s aim and methodology. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Loaves in which up to 20 percent of the wheat flour had been replaced with breadfruit flour received ratings similar to those of all-wheat loaves.
Food scientists in Jamaica, which imports nearly all of its wheat, wanted to know whether flour made from breadfruit, a starchy tree fruit, could replace part of the wheat flour in bread.
The researchers baked loaves containing varying amounts of breadfruit flour and asked fifty volunteers to rate each loaf’s flavor and texture.
To find out whether breadfruit flour could replace some of the wheat flour in bread, food scientists in Jamaica had volunteers rate loaves made with varying amounts of it.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: what the scientists wanted to learn and how they went about it. Choice D gives the aim (whether breadfruit flour could replace some wheat flour) and the method (volunteers rated loaves with different amounts of it).

A.recipe: OG (findings offered for aim and method)
A.why_wrong: It reports what the study found rather than what it set out to learn and how.

B.why_wrong: It gives the scientists’ aim and some background but not their method.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the study was done but not what the scientists wanted to find out.

items.notes: Subject: social and applied science (food security). The study is invented and attributed to unnamed food scientists in Jamaica (WAVE.md, no fact-checking for this skill); the setting is real (breadfruit is widely grown in Jamaica, which imports its wheat). Distractors: OG, PART, PART.

items.subtype: Describe a process to an audience familiar with a technique
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Resist dyeing is a technique in which parts of a cloth are covered so that dye cannot reach them.
• Ajrakh is a textile tradition of Pakistan’s Sindh region and India’s Kutch region.
• Artisans use carved wooden blocks to print a paste of lime and gum onto cotton, then dye it in indigo.
• The cloth is then printed and dyed again, this time with red madder.
• Finished pieces display intricate geometric patterns in deep blue and crimson.
items.stem: The student wants to describe how Ajrakh cloth is made to an audience already familiar with resist dyeing. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Ajrakh artisans use resist dyeing, a technique in which parts of a cloth are covered so that dye cannot reach them, to make patterns in indigo and madder.
Ajrakh, a textile tradition of Pakistan’s Sindh region and India’s Kutch region, features intricate geometric patterns in deep blue and crimson.
To make Ajrakh cloth, artisans block-print a resist paste onto cotton, dye it in indigo, and then print it again and dye it with red madder.
In Ajrakh, as in other kinds of resist dyeing, parts of the cloth are covered with a paste so that the dye cannot reach them.
items.explanation: This audience already knows what resist dyeing is, so the sentence should spend its words on the Ajrakh process. Choice C does: a resist paste is block-printed onto cotton, the cloth is dyed in indigo, then printed again and dyed with madder.

A.why_wrong: It defines resist dyeing for readers who already know it and gives little of the Ajrakh process itself.

B.recipe: OG (where it comes from and how it looks)
B.why_wrong: It describes Ajrakh’s origin and patterns, not how the cloth is made.

D.why_wrong: It explains the general idea of resist dyeing, which the audience knows, and leaves out the blocks, the two dyes and the order of the steps.

items.notes: Subject: arts and crafts (South Asian textiles). Real craft, facts known without a search (block-printed lime and gum resist, indigo then madder, made in Sindh and Kutch). Distractors: AUD, OG, AUD, as in 2.18 where every wrong option re-explains the familiar term.

items.subtype: Make a generalization (claim only)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Spinifex is a spiky grass that grows across much of Australia’s arid interior.
• For thousands of years, Aboriginal Australians have used spinifex resin as an adhesive for attaching stone blades to wooden handles.
• They have also used the grass to thatch shelters.
• In the 2010s, researchers extracted nanofibers from spinifex that can make latex gloves thinner and stronger.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the uses of spinifex. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Spinifex has served a remarkable range of purposes, from traditional toolmaking and construction to modern materials research.
Spinifex resin has been used to attach stone blades to wooden handles, and spinifex nanofibers can make latex gloves thinner and stronger.
Spinifex is a spiky grass that grows across much of the arid interior of Australia.
While Aboriginal Australians have used spinifex for thousands of years, researchers began extracting nanofibers from it only in the 2010s.
items.explanation: A generalization about the uses of spinifex has to rise above the individual cases to a broad claim. Choice A does: the grass has served many purposes, from traditional tools and shelters to modern materials research.

B.why_wrong: It lists two specific uses but never makes a general claim about them.

C.why_wrong: It describes the plant rather than its uses.

D.why_wrong: It contrasts when two groups began using spinifex instead of generalizing about its uses.

items.notes: Subject: natural science and culture (Australian plants). Real uses known without a search (spinifex resin as a hafting adhesive, thatch for shelters, nanocellulose for thinner latex studied at the University of Queensland); no researcher named. Distractors follow 2.12: specifics without the claim, background, contrast of two cases.

items.subtype: Describe a distinctive style
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Remedios Varo (1908–1963) was a Spanish-born painter who settled in Mexico City in 1941.
• Varo’s paintings depict slender figures with heart-shaped faces in dreamlike settings.
• She rendered these scenes in meticulous detail, often including intricate machinery.
• Her painting Creation of the Birds (1957) shows an owl-like figure painting birds that come to life.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the distinctive style of Varo’s paintings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A Spanish-born painter who settled in Mexico City in 1941, Remedios Varo developed a distinctive style for depicting figures.
Varo’s paintings place slender, heart-faced figures in dreamlike settings, rendered in meticulous detail and often featuring intricate machinery.
Varo’s painting Creation of the Birds (1957) shows an owl-like figure painting birds that come to life.
Born in Spain in 1908, the painter Remedios Varo settled in Mexico City in 1941.
items.explanation: Describing Varo’s style means saying what her paintings look like. Choice B does: slender, heart-faced figures in dreamlike settings, painted in meticulous detail and often with intricate machinery.

A.recipe: VAGUE (names a style without describing it)
A.why_wrong: It says Varo had a distinctive style but never says what that style is.

C.why_wrong: It tells what one painting shows, not what distinguishes the style of her paintings.

D.why_wrong: It gives facts about Varo’s life, not about her paintings.

items.notes: Subject: arts (surrealist painting). Real painter, facts known without a search (born in Spain 1908, in Mexico City from 1941, elongated heart-faced figures, fine detail and machinery, Creation of the Birds 1957). Distractors follow 2.4: VAGUE, OG, OG.

items.subtype: Specify who
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Pullman Company once employed thousands of Black men as porters on its railroad sleeping cars.
• In 1925, labor organizer A. Philip Randolph founded a union for them, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters.
• In 1937, the union negotiated a contract with the Pullman Company.
• It was the first labor agreement between a major US corporation and a union led by Black workers.
items.stem: The student wants to specify who founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In 1937, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters negotiated a contract with the Pullman Company.
The Pullman Company once employed thousands of Black men as porters on its railroad sleeping cars.
The Brotherhood’s 1937 contract was the first labor agreement between a major US corporation and a union led by Black workers.
The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters was founded in 1925 by labor organizer A. Philip Randolph.
items.explanation: The goal asks who founded the union. Choice D names him: labor organizer A. Philip Randolph, in 1925.

A.why_wrong: It tells what the union achieved in 1937, not who founded it.

B.why_wrong: It describes the porters’ jobs, not who founded their union.

C.why_wrong: It explains why the 1937 contract mattered, not who founded the union.

items.notes: Subject: history (labor and civil rights). Real union and well-known facts, no search needed (founded by A. Philip Randolph in 1925; 1937 contract with Pullman, the first between a major company and a Black-led union). Distractors all OG, as in SPEC items.

items.subtype: Similarity stated once per entity
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bhutan’s 2008 constitution directs its government to promote Gross National Happiness.
• Bhutan measures progress toward this goal with an index of citizens’ well-being, not just economic output.
• The index covers areas such as health, education, and community life.
• In 2019, New Zealand introduced its first Wellbeing Budget.
• This budget directed government spending according to measures of citizens’ well-being, not just economic output.
• It gave priority to mental health and child poverty.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Bhutan’s pursuit of Gross National Happiness and New Zealand’s Wellbeing Budget. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Bhutan’s constitution called for promoting Gross National Happiness in 2008, whereas New Zealand introduced its first Wellbeing Budget in 2019.
Bhutan’s index of citizens’ well-being covers areas such as health, education, and community life.
Both Bhutan’s pursuit of Gross National Happiness and New Zealand’s Wellbeing Budget rely on measures of citizens’ well-being, not just economic output.
New Zealand’s first Wellbeing Budget, introduced in 2019, gave priority to mental health and child poverty.
items.explanation: The notes describe both countries as looking at citizens’ well-being and not only at economic output. Choice C names both countries and states that shared trait.

A.recipe: REL (a difference offered for a similarity)
A.why_wrong: It contrasts when each country acted instead of stating what their approaches share.

B.why_wrong: It describes Bhutan’s index and does not mention New Zealand.

D.why_wrong: It describes New Zealand’s budget and does not mention Bhutan.

items.notes: Subject: social science (measuring national progress). Real policies known without a search (Bhutan’s 2008 constitution and Gross National Happiness index; New Zealand’s 2019 Wellbeing Budget with mental health and child poverty among its priorities). The shared trait is stated once per entity, as in 1.11.

items.subtype: Describe what a work consists of
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Belgian-born artist Francis Alÿs has lived and worked in Mexico City since the 1980s.
• Many of his artworks are performances staged in urban streets and documented on video.
• In Paradox of Praxis 1 (1997), Alÿs pushed an enormous block of ice through the streets of Mexico City.
• He continued pushing for more than nine hours, until the block had melted into a small puddle.
items.stem: The student wants to describe what Alÿs did in Paradox of Praxis 1. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In Paradox of Praxis 1 (1997), Alÿs pushed an enormous block of ice through Mexico City’s streets for more than nine hours, until it melted into a puddle.
Belgian-born artist Francis Alÿs has lived and worked in Mexico City since the 1980s.
Like many of Francis Alÿs’s artworks, Paradox of Praxis 1 is a performance staged in urban streets and documented on video.
Paradox of Praxis 1 is a 1997 artwork in which an enormous block of ice melted into a small puddle.
items.explanation: The goal asks what Alÿs did in this work. Choice A describes the performance: he pushed a block of ice through Mexico City for more than nine hours until it melted.

B.why_wrong: It tells where Alÿs has lived, not what he did in this work.

C.why_wrong: It says the work is a street performance but not what Alÿs did in it.

D.why_wrong: It says that a block of ice melted but not that Alÿs pushed it through the city.

items.notes: Subject: arts (performance art). Real artist and well-known work, no search needed (Alÿs pushed a block of ice through Mexico City for over nine hours in 1997 until it melted). Distractors: OG, OG, PART.

items.subtype: Explain the origin of a name
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tanzanite is a blue-violet gemstone, a variety of the mineral zoisite prized for its intense color.
• It was discovered in 1967 in the Merelani Hills of northern Tanzania.
• Those hills remain the only known source of tanzanite.
• In 1968, the jewelry company Tiffany & Co. named the gemstone after the country where it was discovered.
items.stem: The student wants to explain the origin of tanzanite’s name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Tanzanite, a blue-violet variety of the mineral zoisite, was discovered in 1967.
Tanzanite was named by Tiffany & Co. after Tanzania, the country where the gem was discovered.
The Merelani Hills of northern Tanzania remain the only known source of tanzanite.
Introduced by the jewelry company Tiffany & Co. in 1968, tanzanite is a gemstone prized for its intense color.
items.explanation: To explain where the name comes from, the sentence must connect it to its source. Choice B does: Tiffany & Co. named the gem after Tanzania, where it was found.

A.why_wrong: It identifies the mineral and the year of discovery but says nothing about the name.

C.why_wrong: It mentions Tanzania but never says that the gem was named after the country.

D.why_wrong: It names the company and the gem but does not say how or why the gem got its name.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (mineralogy). Real gem and well-known facts, no search needed (zoisite variety found in 1967 in the Merelani Hills, the only source; named by Tiffany & Co. in 1968). Distractors all OG; D holds both halves with no link, like 1.6 C.
